order.why_here: The smallest traversal: one start cell, one component, recolouring doubles as the visited mark.
Scan plus flood: every flood launched from an unvisited cell is a new component, so count the launches.
Same scan, but each flood returns how many cells it swallowed; the traversal now produces a value.
Reverse the question: flood from the whole border at once and count what the border never reached.
Same border flood, but with a temporary sentinel mark and a final rewrite sweep of the board.
Two border floods with a directional edge rule (climb uphill); the answer is their intersection.
Multi-source BFS processed layer by layer: each layer is one minute, so the layer count is the answer.
All zeros as one super-source: BFS layers become a distance written into every cell.
Same distance wave from all gates, writing distances in place so the grid is its own visited set.
Leave the grid: a real adjacency-list graph, traversed with an old-node to new-node map as the visited set.
Implicit graph: nodes are words, edges are one-letter changes, and wildcard buckets generate neighbours cheaply.
Keep every shortest path: BFS records a parents DAG layer by layer, then backtracking reads the paths out.
Whole board configurations become nodes; BFS over state strings with a precomputed move table.
Choose the right node: routes, not stops, so one BFS edge is one bus ride.
Clique edges (equal values) would blow up BFS; consume each value bucket once to keep it linear.
BFS over strings where branching is pruned to swaps that fix the first mismatch.
Augment the state with a resource: (row, col, eliminations left) is the node.
Augment the state with a bitmask of keys held; the same cell is a different node per key ring.
Multi-source BFS over (node, visited-mask): TSP-shaped search on a tiny graph.
Two kinds of moves with different cost: free player walks and paid pushes, the first 0-1 BFS.
Directed graphs begin: no traversal at all, just in-degree minus out-degree per node.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove in-degree-0 nodes; leftovers mean a cycle.
Same Kahn loop with the pop order recorded: that order is a topological sort.
Build the directed graph yourself from adjacent word pairs, then topo-sort it (with a prefix trap).
Topological order carries a DP: finish time is the slowest prerequisite plus own duration.
Two-level topo sort: order the groups, then order items inside each group.
Use every edge exactly once: Hierholzer's post-order DFS builds an Eulerian path.
Union-find introduced: each successful union lowers the component count by one.
A tree is n-1 edges and no cycle; union-find reports a cycle the moment a union fails.
Return the edge whose union fails: the first edge that closes a cycle.
Directed version: a node with two parents and a cycle interact, so try candidates in the right order.
Union-find over string keys: shared emails glue accounts, then group by root.
Online union-find on a grid: cells appear one at a time and the island count is updated per addition.
Union-find component sizes plus counting infected nodes per component to choose the best removal.
Union through hub nodes: join each number to its prime factors instead of to every other number.
Union-find over time: group meetings by timestamp and reset components that did not touch the secret.
Offline queries: sort edges and queries by weight and grow one union-find as the threshold rises.
Two union-finds sharing edges; greedily take shared edges first, count the rest as removable.
Weighted edges: Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion of stale entries.
Edge weights only 0 or 1: a deque replaces the heap (0-1 BFS) on a grid.
Change what a path costs: the maximum cell on it (bottleneck), still solved by a heap-driven search.
Three Dijkstras, one on the reversed graph, combined at a meeting node.
Minimum spanning tree: connect everything as cheaply as possible with Prim's heap.
Kruskal run repeatedly with one edge excluded or forced, to classify every edge.
The final boss: Tarjan's DFS low-link finds every bridge in one pass.
